tldr: World models develop rich physical grounding, but their inference is too heavy to run inside robot control loops. This paper distills that physical understanding into compact VLAs using simple feature alignment during training. Without sacrificing any inference speed or memory, a 0.8B student policy approaches the manipulation performance of a 4B model.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed pipeline. On the left, visual features are extracted once from a frozen world model and cached. On the right, the student VLA is trained with an added cosine similarity loss against this cache. The auxiliary projection head is discarded at test time, incurring zero added computational cost during deployment.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are a promising approach for generalist robot control, but they suffer from a fundamental brittleness to minor environmental changes. Conventional VLAs simply map current images and instructions directly to actions. Because they lack an objective that accounts for how the world responds to those actions, they fail to learn physical causality effectively. In contrast, world models that predict future video frames or states acquire excellent physical grounding. However, unrolling future predictions requires seconds per decision, ruling them out of real-time control loops on physical robots.

To bridge this gap, the authors observed that what a world model knows about physical scenes lives inside its internal features, rather than in the generative process itself. Generating future frames is merely the training scaffolding that produces those grounded representations. By transferring only these internal representations to a student policy, one can inherit the world model's physical grounding without paying its heavy inference cost.

In this paper, the authors propose a straightforward distillation method: visual features from a frozen world model are pre-computed and cached to disk, and the compact student VLA is trained with a cosine similarity loss to align its image representations with the cache. The world model is never loaded into GPU memory during VLA training, and the added projector is discarded at deployment. As a result, the model size and inference latency remain completely identical to the undistilled baseline.

Evaluations across simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboCasa-GR1) and physical robot platforms (single-arm and bimanual) show that a compact 0.8B student consistently improves its success rate, approaching the performance of 4B-scale policies.
contributions: Proposed a simple representation-distillation pipeline that transfers the physical grounding of a world model into a compact VLA without adding any test-time computational cost.

Eliminated additional training memory by pre-caching teacher features, and preserved the baseline's model size and inference speed (32 ms on an RTX 5090) by discarding the auxiliary projector at deployment.

Demonstrated that a 0.8B student reaches 97.9% on LIBERO, improves from 48.2% to 50.5% on RoboCasa-GR1, and consistently approaches 4B-class performance across real-world single-arm and bimanual manipulation.

Showed that the performance gains persist across variations in student scale, backbone, alignment layer, and teacher model, confirming that the distillation acts as a broad representational prior rather than a fragile pairing between two specific networks.

sections.heading: Can We Borrow a World Model's Physical Intuition for a Lightweight VLA?
sections.summary: VLAs are vulnerable to out-of-distribution shifts because they do not explicitly learn causal dynamics, while world models possess strong physical grounding but are too slow for real-time control. This paper observes that a world model's physical knowledge lives in its internal features and distills that representation into a lightweight VLA with zero added inference compute.
sections.details:
In robotics, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—adapting large vision-language backbones to predict actions—have taken center stage. Leveraging internet-scale semantic knowledge, they scale across diverse tasks. Yet in deployment, they remain remarkably brittle to common perturbations like camera shifts, lighting variations, or unexpected obstacles.

This brittleness stems from how VLAs are trained. Standard VLAs are optimized to map current observations directly to actions, with no objective that accounts for how the world responds to those actions. Without an incentive to learn causal physical dynamics, the only way to improve robustness has been expensive and exhaustive data collection.

In contrast, world models are trained to predict future frames or states, naturally embedding physical causality and temporal structure into their representations. However, unrolling the future via autoregressive steps or diffusion models is computationally prohibitive. For instance, the recent world-model-based policy DreamZero takes roughly 3 seconds per inference step on an H100 and consumes 45.9 GB of VRAM. A lightweight VLA, by comparison, runs in 32 ms and uses just 1.86 GB on a consumer RTX 5090. World models are compelling repositories of physical knowledge, but they are impractical as deployable policies.

This led the authors to ask: Can we inherit the grounded representations of a large world model without paying its inference cost? Generating the future is merely the training objective that forged those representations; the knowledge of physical scenes already lives inside the internal features. Distilling those features into a student policy allows us to retain the grounding while leaving the heavy generative machinery behind.

The proposed method simply adds a single cache-based feature-alignment loss to standard VLA training. Through this lightweight addition, a tiny 0.8B student achieves robustness and success rates approaching those of 4B-class models in both simulation and real-world experiments.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Compact VLAs, World Models, and Feature Distillation
sections.summary: This section reviews the trend toward scaling and shrinking VLAs, predictive world models and world-action models (WAMs), and representation-level distillation. It frames how this work adapts intermediate-feature alignment to transfer physical dynamics without requiring action-space parity.
sections.details:
To contextualize this work, let us review four relevant lines of research.

### Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs)
Robotics policies have evolved from early models like OpenVLA, which discretize actions into tokens for autoregressive prediction, to continuous flow-matching policies such as GR00T N1 and $\pi_0$ / $\pi_{0.5}$. In parallel, compact VLAs designed for consumer hardware—such as SmolVLA (2.2B), VLA-OS (0.5B), and Seer (0.57B)—have gained traction. However, aggressive downsizing often degrades manipulation accuracy. This work aims to recover that lost accuracy without expanding the inference budget.

### World Models and World Action Models (WAMs)
Foundational video world models include video diffusion transformers like Wan and Cosmos, as well as non-generative, latent-space predictive models like V-JEPA 2. More recently, World Action Models (WAMs) such as Cosmos-Policy, DreamZero, and Fast-WAM unify future-state prediction with action generation. While these models exhibit strong robustness, the compute required to rollout future trajectories remains a bottleneck that hinders real-time control.

### Representation-Level Distillation
Classical knowledge distillation (Hinton et al.) matches the teacher's output probabilities, whereas approaches like FitNets transfer intermediate layer hints. Recently, in generative modeling, REPA demonstrated that aligning intermediate diffusion transformer representations with a self-supervised visual encoder via cosine similarity substantially accelerates training.

This paper adapts the core idea of REPA to robotic world models. The key difference lies in what the teacher knows: video world models have physical causality and temporal dynamics baked directly into their hidden representations. By aligning feature directions, a student VLA absorbs that physical grounding without ever having to generate a future frame.

sections.heading: Embedding a World Model at Zero Inference Cost: How Feature Alignment Works
sections.summary: The proposed approach pre-extracts world-model features over training frames offline and computes a cosine loss against the student VLA's image tokens. Because no action targets are shared with the teacher and the projection head is dropped at deployment, test-time speed and memory remain completely identical to the compact baseline.
sections.details:
The design of the proposed method is strikingly simple. As shown in Figure F2, it adds a single feature-alignment loss to an existing VLA training pipeline, aligning the student's visual tokens with those of a frozen world model.

### III-A Student Architecture and the Base Action Loss
The student, designated QwenGR00T, pairs a Qwen3.5-VL (0.8B) backbone with a GR00T-style flow-matching action expert. Given an observation $\mathbf{o}_t$ (multi-camera views, a language instruction, and proprioceptive states), the backbone outputs final-layer hidden representations $h(\mathbf{o}_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times D_s}$. The action expert is trained via flow matching to regress vector fields along linear interpolation paths between Gaussian noise and target action trajectories (Equation 1, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}$).

Crucially, action supervision comes solely from ground-truth demonstration trajectories; no action labels are inherited from the world model. Because world models and VLAs often parameterize actions differently, tying the distillation to action spaces would restrict generality. All knowledge transfer occurs strictly through the visual representations.

### III-B World-Model Representation Alignment Loss
For each camera view $c \in \mathcal{C}$, the hidden states corresponding to visual tokens are mean-pooled into a single vector $f^S_c$. This vector passes through a 2-layer MLP projector $p_\phi$ to match the teacher's dimension $D_t$, and a cosine distance loss is computed against the teacher feature $f^T_c$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|} \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \left( 1 - \cos(p_\phi(f^S_c), \mathrm{sg}[f^T_c]) \right)$$

The total training loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{align}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}$, where $\lambda_{\mathrm{align}} = 0.5$ across all experiments. Enforcing directional alignment (cosine similarity) rather than strict magnitude matching prevents the distillation objective from overriding the feature geometry required for action generation.

### Efficiency via Offline Caching
Because the teacher is completely frozen, its features over the training dataset are computed once and stored on disk as a memory-mapped cache. During VLA training, the massive world model never needs to reside in GPU memory, preserving the baseline's batch size and hardware requirements. At test time, the projector $p_\phi$ is discarded. The deployed policy's architecture, memory footprint, and inference latency remain identical to the original small VLA (32 ms on an RTX 5090).

### III-C Teacher Model: Cosmos3-Nano
The primary teacher is the understanding tower of the Cosmos 3 multimodal world model (based on Qwen3-VL-8B). Features are mean-pooled from the 24th layer hidden states of the visual tokens ($D_t = 4096$). Because this understanding tower runs deterministically, it avoids the sampling variance inherent to diffusion rollouts.

captions.F2: Overview of the proposed framework. In Step 1 (left), the frozen teacher world model is run offline once to extract and cache per-camera visual representations. In Step 2 (right), the student VLA is trained with standard flow-matching action loss alongside a cosine alignment loss between its final visual features and the cached teacher representations.

sections.heading: Simulation and Real-Robot Tests: A 0.8B Policy Narrows the Gap to 4B Models
sections.summary: The method was evaluated across LIBERO, humanoid manipulation in RoboCasa-GR1, and real-world single-arm and bimanual tasks. The 0.8B student consistently outperformed the undistilled baseline and achieved success rates rivaling a 4B policy with five times more parameters. Extensive ablations confirm the gain acts as a general representational prior.
sections.details:
To validate the approach, the authors conducted experiments across two simulation benchmarks and two physical robot setups.

### IV-A & IV-B LIBERO Benchmark
Evaluated across all four LIBERO suites, performance is reported as the average over four independent evaluation runs combining two seeds and two GPU platforms (A100 and RTX 5090). The 0.8B student with feature alignment achieved a 97.9% average success rate, gaining +2.6 points over the identical undistilled baseline (95.3%). While existing sub-4B policies range between 78.7% and 95.3%, this 0.8B student sets a new high mark.

### IV-C RoboCasa-GR1 (Full-Body Humanoid Manipulation)
In RoboCasa-GR1, evaluating a GR1 humanoid across 24 environments with a single egocentric camera and a 29-DoF bimanual action space, the proposed distillation boosted the 0.8B model from 48.2% to 50.5% (+2.3 points). This outpaces alternative architectures such as QwenFAST, QwenPI, and Isaac-GR00T, closing the gap to the 5x larger 4B baseline (54.8%) to within 4.3 points. Rather than deploying massive human-video pre-trained models, borrowing representations from an existing world model effectively bridges the capability divide.

### IV-D Real-Robot Experiments (Single-Arm and Bimanual)
Real-world evaluations tested three tasks (30 trials per condition): fruit pick-and-place and egg pick-and-place on an AgileX Nero (7-DoF single arm), and fruit handoff-to-bag on TRIP-Bag (7-DoF bimanual). Representative successful rollouts are shown in Figure F3.

- Fruit Pick-and-Place (Single-Arm): Distillation improved success from 83.3% (25/30) to 93.3% (28/30), matching the 4B model (93.3%).
- Egg Pick-and-Place (Single-Arm): On fragile, low-friction eggs requiring delicate force modulation, distillation lifted the baseline from 46.7% (14/30) to 60.0% (18/30), significantly closing the gap to the 4B model (70.0%).
- Bimanual Handoff (TRIP-Bag): On this coordination-heavy task, the student improved from 40.0% to 46.7% (compared to 53.3% for the 4B model).

Failure analysis (Figure F4) revealed that mistakes were rarely semantic misidentifications. Instead, they stemmed from precision boundaries within the final centimeters of physical contact—such as clipping the basket rim or dropping slippery eggs. This confirms that the world model's representations effectively supply high-level scene understanding and spatial guidance.

### IV-E Ablations
Ablations dissected the sources of these improvements:

- Student Scale and Backbone: Distillation consistently improved performance when scaling the student to 4B (+1.9 points) or switching to an alternative 1B vision-language backbone (+3.0 points).
- Alignment Depth: Aligning at 1/3 depth, mid-depth, 2/3 depth, and the final layer showed that the final layer yielded the highest success (49.8%), though mid-depth was close behind (49.4%). Aligning the final layer is computationally optimal because its outputs feed directly into the action head.
- Teacher Diversity: Replacing Cosmos3-Nano with Fast-WAM (a Wan2.2-based video diffusion transformer) or V-JEPA2-AC (a self-supervised latent predictive model) still surpassed the undistilled baseline (96.9% and 96.5% vs. 95.3%). This proves the effect is not a fluke of one network pair, but a general benefit of world-model representations.

captions.F3: Successful real-robot executions using the distilled 0.8B student policy: (a) single-arm fruit pick-and-place on AgileX Nero, (b) delicate egg pick-and-place, and (c) bimanual mid-air fruit handoff and bagging on TRIP-Bag.
captions.F4: Primary failure modes observed during physical robot experiments: (a) dropping the object before clearing the basket, (b) grasping the rim instead of the fruit, (c) slipping while lifting the egg, and (d) dropping the egg mid-transit. Most failures were driven by contact and grasping limits rather than semantic errors.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Dropping Heavy Generation to Keep Pure Physical Grounding
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that feature alignment provides a practical bridge between the rich physical reasoning of heavy world models and the nimble inference of lightweight VLAs. It offers an effective recipe for boosting small robot policies without conceding a single millisecond of latency or megabyte of memory.
sections.details:
World models develop strong physical grounding by predicting the future, but the compute cost of future rollouts has historically kept them out of real-time control loops. This paper proves that physical representation and generative rollout can be fully disentangled.

By aligning a VLA's visual representations with a frozen world model offline during training, the deployed policy runs as a completely unmodified, lightweight network while reaping the benefits of grounded physical representations. There is zero increase in latency and zero memory overhead at deployment.

While the improvements are steady rather than overwhelming (around 2 to 3 percentage points), they manifest reliably across simulation suites (LIBERO, RoboCasa-GR1) and physical robot platforms (both single-arm and bimanual). Furthermore, because these gains persist across different student sizes, backbones, alignment layers, and teacher architectures, the distillation acts as a robust representational prior rather than an overfitted pairing.

For roboticists aiming to deploy responsive, physically capable policies on edge hardware or consumer GPUs, this provides an actionable and clean design pattern.

takeaways: A world model's physical grounding resides within its internal representations; its benefits can be extracted via feature distillation without running costly future rollouts.
Pre-caching teacher representations offline and training with a cosine alignment loss adds zero GPU memory overhead during training and zero inference overhead at deployment.
The approach is broadly architecture-agnostic, functioning effectively across different student scales and backbones, as well as distinct teacher models (Cosmos, Fast-WAM, V-JEPA 2).
Infusing world-model grounding enables a lightweight 0.8B VLA to achieve manipulation accuracy that rivals policies with multiple times more parameters.
limitations: While the 2–3 point performance gains are consistent, the compact student does not fully surpass massive frontier models pre-trained on specialized proprietary datasets.
As highlighted in the failure analysis, visual representation alignment alone cannot resolve sub-millimeter physical contact challenges, such as delicate low-friction grasping and fine force control.
Pre-computing and caching the teacher representations introduces upfront storage requirements and initial computational overhead (e.g., approximately 1 hour on 4 GPUs for LIBERO).
